structured_output.hypothesis: If domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species, dog genomes will not nest as a single clade inside one wild species but will show substantial genome-wide ancestry from at least two separate wild Canis species (e.g. gray wolf plus a jackal or coyote lineage).
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using whole-genome sequence of dog (Canis lupus familiaris, CanFam3.1 and linked resequencing), gray wolf, coyote (C. latrans), golden jackal (C. aureus) and an outgroup, ABBA-BABA D-statistics for ((wolf, dog), non-wolf Canis species, outgroup) show significant excess allele sharing between dog and the non-wolf species relative to wolf (block-jackknife |Z| > 3 and |D| >= 0.05), AND the estimated non-wolf ancestry fraction in dogs is >= 10% of the genome.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Dog genomes nest inside gray wolf variation, non-wolf Canis species share alleles equally with dog and wolf (|D| < 0.05 or |Z| < 3), and estimated non-wolf ancestry in dogs is < 2% of the genome. Then dogs descend from a single wild species and the claim is refuted. Intermediate results (2-10% ancestry) count as inconclusive.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's "wild species" is read as distinct biological species in the modern sense (reproductively separate Canis species such as gray wolf, golden jackal, coyote), and "descended from" as ancestral genomic contribution. Darwin's "geographical and other considerations" (regional dog types resembling local wild canids) are replaced by genome-wide allele sharing. Dog-wolf gene flow is within one species (C. lupus) and does not count. Limitation: the landing page is the NCBI dog reference assembly; the other canid assemblies and SRA reads must be taken from linked NCBI records, so the reference is the alignment anchor rather than a complete test set on its own.
